questions.question: How does Elasticsearch differ from PostgreSQL for search?
questions.title: Elasticsearch vs PostgreSQL for Search
questions.direct_answer: Elasticsearch is **purpose-built for full-text search and analytics** with an **inverted index**, **relevance scoring**, and near real-time search across large datasets. PostgreSQL supports full-text search via tsvector and GIN indexes, but lacks relevance tuning, distributed horizontal scaling, and the rich query DSL that Elasticsearch provides. For simple keyword search on small datasets, PostgreSQL is sufficient; for complex, relevance-ranked, or large-scale search, use Elasticsearch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that Elasticsearch is a specialized search engine optimized for a different problem than a relational database, and can articulate when each is the right choice.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Elasticsearch as a general-purpose database or as a drop-in replacement for PostgreSQL. Elasticsearch lacks full ACID transactions and is not suitable as a primary data store.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the dual-write pattern -- writing to PostgreSQL as the source of truth and syncing to Elasticsearch for search -- and how to handle consistency between the two.

sections.title: Two Different Tools for Two Different Jobs
sections.content: Elasticsearch and PostgreSQL serve different primary purposes. PostgreSQL is a relational database with ACID transactions, joins, and normalized data storage. Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene, optimized for full-text search with relevance scoring, faceted filtering, and horizontal scalability across billions of documents.

sections.title: PostgreSQL vs Elasticsearch — Head to Head
sections.content:
| Dimension | PostgreSQL | Elasticsearch |
|---|---|---|
| Primary Use Case | Relational data, ACID transactions ✅ | Full-text search, analytics ✅ |
| Data Model | Normalized tables with schemas ✅ | JSON documents, dynamic mapping ⚠️ |
| Full-Text Search | tsvector + GIN index (basic) ⚠️ | Inverted index with relevance scoring ✅ |
| Relevance Scoring | Not supported ❌ | BM25 + custom scoring ✅ |
| Horizontal Scale | Difficult (sharding required) ⚠️ | Built-in sharding and replication ✅ |
| ACID Transactions | Full support ✅ | Not supported ❌ |
| Joins | Native SQL joins ✅ | Application-level only ❌ |
| Aggregations/Facets | GROUP BY (row-scan) ⚠️ | Native, fast aggregations ✅ |
| Consistency | Strong (immediate) ✅ | Near real-time (1s refresh) ⚠️ |

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content: Use PostgreSQL for search when: your dataset is small (under a few million rows); search queries are simple keyword matches; you cannot afford to maintain a separate search service; full ACID consistency on search results is required. Use Elasticsearch when: you need relevance-ranked results with BM25 scoring; users expect Google-style search with typo tolerance, stemming, and synonyms; you need faceted filtering (filter by category AND price range AND rating simultaneously); your dataset is large and query latency must stay under 100ms. In production, most systems use PostgreSQL as the source of truth and Elasticsearch as a read-optimized search layer, with a sync mechanism between them.

sections.title: Integrating Elasticsearch Alongside PostgreSQL in Spring Boot
sections.content:
In production Java applications, Elasticsearch and PostgreSQL typically work together rather than replacing each other. PostgreSQL remains the source of truth for transactional data; Elasticsearch serves as a read-optimized search index derived from that data.

**The dual-write problem.** The simplest approach — writing to both PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch in the same request — is fragile. If the Elasticsearch write fails after the PostgreSQL commit, your search index is stale. If you wrap both in a distributed transaction, latency increases and availability decreases. The recommended pattern is **Change Data Capture (CDC):** use Debezium to stream PostgreSQL WAL changes to Kafka, then a consumer writes to Elasticsearch. This guarantees eventual consistency without coupling application code to the indexing pipeline.

```
PostgreSQL → (WAL) → Debezium → Kafka → Consumer → Elasticsearch
```

**Simpler alternative for smaller systems.** If CDC infrastructure is overkill, use an application-level event: after saving to PostgreSQL, publish a Spring `ApplicationEvent` that an async listener picks up and indexes into Elasticsearch. Pair this with a scheduled full reindex job (e.g., nightly) to catch any missed events. This is not as reliable as CDC but works well for systems where minutes of staleness are acceptable.

**Query routing in the service layer.** Build your repository layer so simple lookups by ID or foreign key go to PostgreSQL (fast primary-key lookup, strong consistency), while full-text search, faceted filtering, and autocomplete queries go to Elasticsearch. Spring Data provides both `JpaRepository` and `ElasticsearchRepository` — expose a service that delegates to the right one based on query type. This keeps the search index focused on what it does best rather than duplicating every database query.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PostgreSQL FTS for simple keyword search on existing data** — GIN index on tsvector; no sync pipeline; no separate service; sufficient for millions of documents with basic relevance needs
- **Elasticsearch for fuzzy matching, autocomplete, and complex relevance** — edge n-gram tokenizers for autocomplete; `fuzziness: AUTO` for typo tolerance; field boosting for custom relevance; built-in, not tacked on
- **Elasticsearch scales search horizontally** — shards distributed across nodes; hundreds of millions of documents with thousands of search queries per second; PostgreSQL single-instance can't match this at the top end
- **Sync pipeline is the Elasticsearch operational cost** — dual-write, CDC, or ETL keeps Elasticsearch in sync with the primary database; each approach has failure modes that PostgreSQL FTS avoids by being the primary store
- **Start with PostgreSQL FTS; migrate when requirements outgrow it** — validate that fuzzy search, autocomplete, or horizontal search scale are actually needed before adding the operational overhead of a separate cluster

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch solve different problems. PostgreSQL is a relational database with full-text search as an added feature; Elasticsearch is a search engine first that happens to store documents. The question is whether your search requirements justify the operational cost of a separate service.

**Where PostgreSQL full-text search is sufficient**
- PostgreSQL's `tsvector` and `tsquery` with a GIN index provide fast keyword search, stemming, and basic relevance ranking on millions of documents — no separate service to operate, no sync pipeline to maintain
- For a simple "search posts by keyword" feature on a moderately-sized dataset (up to a few million rows), PostgreSQL FTS is often enough and the simpler choice

**Where Elasticsearch wins**
- Elasticsearch is built around an inverted index optimized for search — it handles fuzzy matching (`fuzziness: AUTO`), autocomplete (edge n-gram analyzers), multi-field relevance tuning (field boosting), and faceted navigation (aggregations) naturally, whereas each of these requires significant custom PostgreSQL work
- At hundreds of millions of documents or high search query volume (thousands of search requests per second), Elasticsearch's distributed architecture scales horizontally in ways a single PostgreSQL instance cannot
- Complex relevance scoring — boosting recent articles, penalizing low-engagement posts, combining BM25 scores with custom signals — is expressed as a query in Elasticsearch and would require custom SQL functions and application-level sorting in PostgreSQL

**The operational cost**
- Elasticsearch requires a sync pipeline — writes go to PostgreSQL (the source of truth) and must be replicated to Elasticsearch; dual-write from the application, CDC via Debezium, or a scheduled sync job each have failure modes
- For a startup or small team, that operational overhead often isn't justified until the search requirements outgrow PostgreSQL FTS

questions.question: What is an Elasticsearch index mapping and how do you configure it?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Index Mapping: What It Is and How to Configure It
questions.direct_answer: An Elasticsearch index **mapping defines the schema** for documents in that index -- the field names, their data types (**text, keyword, date, integer, nested**, etc.), and **how each field is analyzed** at index and query time. Configuring mapping explicitly prevents dynamic mapping from making wrong type inferences, ensures efficient storage, and controls which fields are searchable, sortable, or aggregatable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between text and keyword field types, the role of analyzers in text fields, and why you should always define explicit mappings in production.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using dynamic mapping in production and discovering that Elasticsearch inferred a field as text when you needed keyword (for exact-match filtering or aggregations), or vice versa.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain multi-fields -- mapping a single field as both text (for full-text search) and keyword (for sorting and aggregations) simultaneously.

sections.title: Mapping as Schema
sections.content: A mapping in Elasticsearch is equivalent to a table schema in SQL. It defines every field's data type and indexing behavior. The two most critical field types are text -- which is analyzed (tokenized, lowercased, stemmed) for full-text search -- and keyword -- which is stored as-is for exact-match filtering, sorting, and aggregations. A field can only be one type at the top level, but multi-fields allow mapping the same value as both.

sections.title: Explicit Mapping with Custom Analyzer
Production Mapping Practices
sections.content: After an index is live, most mapping changes require a reindex: Elasticsearch cannot reinterpret already-indexed values as a new core type. Production teams therefore version indices (`products_v2`), use the Reindex API or alias swaps for cutover, and guard string explosion with `ignore_above` on `keyword` subfields. Dynamic mapping is fine for sandboxes; in prod, lock down `dynamic` to `strict` on sensitive indices so a typo never creates a high-cardinality field that balloons cluster state. When you need both fuzzy search and exact SKU filters, reach for multi-fields rather than duplicating the same business value in two top-level properties.

sections.title: Field Mapping Strategies and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
Elasticsearch mapping decisions made at index creation time have a lasting impact on search quality and performance. Unlike a relational schema, changing a field's type after indexing requires reindexing all documents.

**Dynamic vs explicit mapping.** By default, Elasticsearch dynamically maps fields when the first document is indexed: strings become both `text` (analyzed, searchable) and `keyword` (exact match, aggregatable) via multi-fields.
- This is convenient for development but wasteful in production — every string field gets two inverted indexes, doubling storage.
- Set `dynamic: strict` on production indices to reject documents with unmapped fields, forcing developers to declare mappings explicitly.

**Choosing the right field type.** Use `text` for fields that need full-text search (product descriptions, article bodies).
- Use `keyword` for fields that need exact matching, sorting, or aggregation (status codes, email addresses, tags).
- Use `date` with an explicit format for timestamps.
- Use `nested` for arrays of objects that need independent querying (e.g., finding a product where one variant has color=red AND size=large — a flat object array would match color=red on one variant and size=large on another).

**Analyzers at mapping time vs query time.** The `analyzer` property on a text field controls how content is tokenized at index time.
- The `search_analyzer` (if different) controls how the query string is tokenized.
- A common pattern for autocomplete is to use an `edge_ngram` analyzer at index time (producing prefix tokens) but a `standard` analyzer at search time (matching the user's full typed term against those prefixes).
- Getting this wrong leads to either too many results (both sides generate ngrams) or zero results (mismatched tokenization).

**Index templates for time-series indices.** When creating date-partitioned indices (e.g., `logs-2026-04-12`), use index templates that automatically apply the correct mapping to any index matching the pattern `logs-*`. This prevents mapping drift across indices and ensures consistent search behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Explicit mapping before indexing production data** — dynamic mapping infers types from the first document; a malformed document creates the wrong type for the field permanently until re-index
- **`text` for full-text search; `keyword` for filtering, sorting, aggregation** — `match` queries on `text`; `term` queries and aggregations on `keyword`; mapping a filterable field as `text` breaks filtering
- **`number_of_shards` is immutable after index creation** — plan the shard count before indexing; target 20-30GB per shard; use the `_shrink` or `_split` API if the initial estimate is wrong
- **`number_of_replicas` can change anytime** — set to 0 during bulk indexing for speed, then restore to 1 after; read requests are served by both primaries and replicas
- **Re-index required for mapping changes** — the `_reindex` API copies documents to a new index with the updated mapping; use index aliases to switch traffic to the new index with zero downtime

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An Elasticsearch index mapping defines how documents are structured and how each field is indexed — which fields are searchable, which are filterable, and what data type is used for each.

**Dynamic vs explicit mapping**
- Without an explicit mapping, Elasticsearch infers types from the first document — a string field gets both `text` (analyzed, full-text searchable) and `keyword` (exact match, sortable) sub-fields by default
- Dynamic mapping is convenient for prototyping but risky in production — if a malformed document is indexed first, the wrong type is inferred and subsequent correct documents may fail or store incorrectly
- Define explicit mappings before indexing production data: `PUT /products/_mapping { "properties": { "name": { "type": "text" }, "status": { "type": "keyword" } } }`

**`text` vs `keyword` — the critical distinction**
- `text` fields are analyzed — the analyzer tokenizes the value and indexes each token, which means `match` queries work for partial matches and the text is not suitable for sorting or aggregation
- `keyword` fields are stored as-is — used for exact match (`term` queries), filtering, sorting, and aggregations; `status = "active"` must be a `keyword` field, not `text`
- The common mistake: mapping a field that you'll filter and aggregate on (like `status`, `category`, `user_id`) as `text` instead of `keyword`; text fields can't be used for exact filtering or aggregations

**Index settings — analysis and performance**
- `number_of_shards` is set at index creation and cannot be changed — choose based on expected document count; a shard that grows beyond 50GB performs poorly; plan for 20-30GB per shard as a target
- `number_of_replicas` can be changed anytime — 1 replica per primary is the standard for production; replicas serve read requests and provide failover

Changing a field's mapping after indexing requires re-indexing the data — the `_reindex` API copies documents from one index to another with the new mapping applied.

questions.question: What types of queries does Elasticsearch support -- match vs term vs bool?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Query Types: match vs term vs bool
questions.direct_answer: Elasticsearch supports two fundamental query categories: **full-text queries** (match, match_phrase, multi_match) that analyze the query string using the same analyzer as the indexed field, and **term-level queries** (term, terms, range, exists) that perform exact, unanalyzed lookups. The **bool query** is a compound query that combines any number of must, should, must_not, and filter clauses to build complex queries.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the analyzed vs exact-match distinction and can choose the right query type for a given search requirement without over-reaching for match when term is sufficient.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using match on a keyword field (no-op because keyword is not analyzed) or using term on a text field (misses due to tokenization -- 'New York' becomes two terms, not one).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the filter vs query context distinction in bool queries: queries in filter context do not compute a relevance score and are cached by Elasticsearch, making them faster for non-ranked filtering.

sections.title: Two Families of Queries
sections.content: Elasticsearch queries fall into two main families: full-text queries that analyze their input before searching (and produce relevance scores), and term-level queries that perform exact lookups without analysis. The bool query composes these into complex logic. Understanding which family to use for a given field type is the most common source of subtle bugs in Elasticsearch applications.

sections.title: Full-Text Queries (analyzed)
sections.content: match: The standard full-text query. Analyzes the query string using the field's analyzer before searching. Use on text fields. match_phrase: Requires terms to appear in the exact order and adjacent to each other (or within a configurable slop). Use for phrase search on text fields. multi_match: Runs a match query across multiple fields simultaneously, with optional field boosting (title^3 to weight title matches higher). match_all: Returns all documents with equal score. Useful for listing all documents without filtering.

sections.title: Term-Level Queries (exact, not analyzed)
sections.content: term: Exact match on a single value. Use on keyword, numeric, boolean, and date fields -- never on text fields. terms: Exact match on any of a list of values (SQL IN equivalent). range: Matches documents where a field value falls within a range (gt, gte, lt, lte). Use on date, numeric, or keyword fields. exists: Returns documents where a field has any non-null value. prefix, wildcard, regexp: Pattern matching on keyword fields. Expensive -- avoid on high-cardinality fields or use sparingly.

sections.title: Compound Queries (bool)
sections.content: bool combines clauses with four operators. must: The clause must match; contributes to the relevance score. should: The clause is optional but boosts score if it matches; at least one must match if there are no must clauses. must_not: The clause must not match; executed in filter context (no scoring, cached). filter: The clause must match but does NOT affect the relevance score; executed in filter context (cached by Elasticsearch for repeated use). Best practice: put all non-scoring conditions (date ranges, category filters, status filters) in filter context for better performance.

sections.title: Query Examples
Advanced Query Patterns — function_score, dis_max, and Span Queries for Complex Relevance
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`match` analyzes the query; `term` does not** — `match` on `text` fields; `term` on `keyword` fields; using `term` on a `text` field returns nothing because the indexed tokens are lowercase and stemmed, not the original value
- **`match_phrase` requires adjacent terms in order** — `"spring boot"` as a phrase; `match` with `operator: AND` requires both terms but not adjacency or order
- **`bool.filter` for filtering conditions** — filter clauses don't affect relevance score and are cached by Elasticsearch; use `filter` for status, date, and ID conditions; use `must` only when the condition should influence relevance
- **`bool.should` boosts relevance without requiring a match** — documents that match `should` clauses score higher; combine with `minimum_should_match` to require at least one
- **`"explain": true` in the query reveals why documents match or don't** — shows term analysis, per-clause scores, and the final BM25 score; the fastest way to debug unexpected results

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Elasticsearch query types split into two families based on whether they analyze their input before searching. Understanding which family a query belongs to prevents a common class of "why does my query return no results?" bugs.

**Full-text queries — analyzed input**
- `match` analyzes the query string through the same analyzer used to index the field — `match: { body: "Spring Boot" }` tokenizes to `["spring", "boot"]` and finds documents containing either or both terms
- `match_phrase` requires terms to appear adjacent and in order — `match_phrase: { body: "spring boot" }` only matches documents where "spring" is immediately followed by "boot"
- Use `match` on `text` fields; the analyzer handles stemming and lowercasing automatically

**Term-level queries — exact match, no analysis**
- `term` finds documents where a field contains the exact specified value — `term: { status: "active" }` searches for the literal string "active" with no analysis
- Use `term` on `keyword` fields; using `term` on a `text` field often returns nothing because the indexed tokens are lowercase stemmed versions, not the original text
- `terms` allows multiple exact values: `terms: { status: ["active", "pending"] }` — equivalent to SQL's `IN` clause

**bool query — combining conditions**
- `bool` is the query used to combine multiple conditions: `must` (equivalent to AND, contributes to relevance score), `should` (equivalent to OR, boosts relevance), `filter` (equivalent to AND, does not affect score, cacheable), and `must_not`
- Always put filtering conditions (status, date range, user_id) in `filter` instead of `must` — filter clauses are cached by Elasticsearch and don't affect the relevance score, which means subsequent identical filter conditions are resolved from cache

Run queries in Kibana's Dev Tools with `"explain": true` to see exactly how terms are analyzed and why a document does or does not match.

sections.title: Spring Data Elasticsearch at a Glance
sections.content: Spring Data Elasticsearch integrates Elasticsearch into Spring Boot using familiar repository patterns. The @Document annotation defines the index name and settings, @Field annotations configure field types and analyzers, and ElasticsearchRepository provides CRUD and derived query method support. For complex queries, ElasticsearchOperations offers full access to the Elasticsearch query DSL.

sections.title: Step 1: Add Dependencies and Configure Connection
sections.content:
Add spring-boot-starter-data-elasticsearch to pom.xml. Configure the cluster URI and credentials in application.properties:

spring.elasticsearch.uris=http://localhost:9200
spring.elasticsearch.username=elastic
spring.elasticsearch.password=changeme

For Spring Boot 3.x, this autoconfigures an ElasticsearchClient and ReactiveElasticsearchClient using the modern transport layer.

Step 3: Create the Repository and Query Methods

Step 5: Production Concerns — Bulk Operations, Retries, and Index Migration
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Document(indexName = "products")` maps the class to an Elasticsearch index** — Spring Data creates the index on startup using the field-level `@Field` annotations for mapping
- **`@Field(type = FieldType.Keyword)` for filter fields** — `keyword` for status, category, user_id; `text` for full-text searchable fields; wrong type causes silent query failures
- **`ElasticsearchRepository` for simple CRUD and derived queries** — extend it for `save()`, `findById()`, and method-name-derived queries; covers the majority of simple use cases
- **`ElasticsearchRestTemplate` for bool queries and aggregations** — derived methods can't express `filter` clauses, nested queries, or aggregation pipelines; use the template with `NativeSearchQueryBuilder` for full control
- **Alias-based index management for zero-downtime re-index** — point an alias at the active index; re-index into a new index with updated mapping; switch the alias; traffic moves without downtime or code change

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Data Elasticsearch provides repository-style integration with Elasticsearch through the Elasticsearch REST client, with support for derived query methods, `@Query` annotations, and the native client for full query control.

**Setup**
- Add `spring-boot-starter-data-elasticsearch`; configure `spring.elasticsearch.uris=http://localhost:9200`; the auto-configuration wires the `ElasticsearchClient` and `ElasticsearchRestTemplate`
- Annotate your model with `@Document(indexName = "products")` and field-level mappings with `@Field(type = FieldType.Text)` or `@Field(type = FieldType.Keyword)`; Spring Data creates the index with the declared mapping on startup if it doesn't exist

**Repository layer**
- Extend `ElasticsearchRepository<Product, String>` — you get `save()`, `findById()`, `deleteById()`, and derived query methods for free
- `findByNameAndStatus(String name, String status)` generates a `bool.must` query with `match` on name and `term` on status — Spring Data infers the query from the method name

**`ElasticsearchRestTemplate` for complex queries**
- When derived methods can't express the query — bool with filter, nested aggregations, script score — use `ElasticsearchRestTemplate.search(NativeSearchQuery, Class<T>)`
- Build the query with `NativeSearchQueryBuilder`: `new NativeSearchQueryBuilder().withQuery(QueryBuilders.boolQuery().must(matchQuery("name", name)).filter(termQuery("status", "active"))).build()`

**Managing index lifecycle**
- Use `@Setting` to configure the analyzer at the index level — define a custom analyzer with edge n-gram tokenizer for autocomplete queries
- Re-indexing: create a new index with the updated mapping, use `_reindex` to copy documents, then update the alias; Spring Data's `IndexOperations.reindex()` wraps this flow

questions.question: What is an inverted index and how does it enable full-text search?
questions.title: Inverted Index: The Foundation of Full-Text Search
questions.direct_answer: An **inverted index** is a data structure that **maps each unique term to the list of documents** containing that term. It is the inverse of a document-centric forward index (document -> words). During indexing, text is analyzed into terms and recorded in the inverted index. At query time, the engine looks up the query terms in the index and retrieves the matching document IDs in **microseconds**, regardless of the total number of documents.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the core data structure that makes search engines fast and can explain why it is fundamentally different from a SQL LIKE query.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing an inverted index with a regular database index. A B-tree index on a text column speeds up exact prefix matches but cannot efficiently retrieve all documents containing a specific word in any position.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain term frequency (TF) and inverse document frequency (IDF) and how they combine in BM25 to score documents, rewarding rare terms that appear many times in a short document.

sections.title: Forward Index vs Inverted Index
sections.content: A forward index maps documents to the words they contain. An inverted index reverses this: it maps each word to the documents that contain it, along with position and frequency information. This reversal is what makes full-text search fast -- instead of scanning every document to find which ones contain a word, the engine performs a direct lookup in the inverted index and retrieves the answer immediately.

sections.title: Building and Querying an Inverted Index
How Lucene Stores the Inverted Index — Segments, Skip Lists, and FSTs
sections.content:
Understanding how Lucene physically stores the inverted index explains why Elasticsearch is fast even on terabyte-scale corpuses, and reveals the tuning knobs that matter in production.

**Segments — immutable mini-indexes**.
- A Lucene index is a collection of immutable segments.
- Each segment is a small, self-contained inverted index.
- New documents are written to a new segment, not appended to existing ones.
- This immutability is fundamental: once written, segment files never change, which means readers can scan them without locks and operating systems can cache them aggressively.
- Updates are implemented as delete-plus-insert across segments — the old document is marked deleted (in a separate `.liv` file) and a new version is added to the current segment.

Background processes periodically merge smaller segments into larger ones, reclaiming space from deleted documents.
- Too many small segments hurts query performance (each segment is searched separately); too aggressive merging hurts write performance.
- The `index.merge.policy` settings tune this balance.
- For write-heavy workloads, larger `max_merged_segment` values reduce merge frequency; for query-heavy workloads, more aggressive merging produces fewer, larger segments that are faster to search.

**The term dictionary uses Finite State Transducers (FSTs)**.
- Inside each segment, the term dictionary is stored as a compact FST — a compressed trie that maps terms to their posting list locations.
- FSTs are extraordinarily memory-efficient: a million unique terms might fit in 10MB instead of 100MB for a naive hash map.
- The FST is loaded into memory at startup, which is why Elasticsearch's heap usage scales with the unique-term count rather than total document count.
- This is also why a poorly-chosen analyzer that creates millions of unique tokens (e.g., raw user IDs as text) can blow out memory — each unique term consumes FST memory.

**Posting lists use skip lists**.
- Each posting list (the list of doc IDs containing a term) is a delta-compressed sequence with skip pointers at regular intervals.
- To answer `WHERE term1 AND term2`, Lucene walks both posting lists simultaneously, using the skip pointers to jump past doc IDs that can't possibly match.
- For two posting lists of 10M doc IDs each, the AND operation might examine only 100K positions because of skip-list short-circuiting.

**Doc values for sorting and aggregations**.
- The inverted index is optimized for "given a term, find documents.
- Sorting and aggregating require the opposite: "given a document, find values.
- Lucene maintains parallel **doc values** — column-oriented storage of field values — specifically for these operations.
- Doc values are stored on disk and memory-mapped, providing fast columnar access without using JVM heap.
- This is why aggregations on a `keyword` field with `doc_values: true` (the default) are fast even on billion-document indexes.

**Refresh and visibility**.
- New documents aren't immediately searchable — they sit in an in-memory buffer until the next refresh (default 1 second), which writes them to a new segment.
- This is why Elasticsearch is often called "near real-time" rather than real-time: there's a configurable lag between write and search visibility.
- Setting `refresh=wait_for` on a write request waits for the next refresh before returning, providing read-your-writes consistency at the cost of higher write latency.
- For bulk indexing, set `index.refresh_interval=-1` to disable refresh entirely until the bulk load completes, then re-enable to make all new documents searchable at once.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Inverted index maps terms to document lists** — searching for "boot" is a term dictionary lookup to `[doc:1, doc:3, ...]`; O(1) lookup + O(k) retrieval; a forward index would require O(n) scan over all documents
- **Analyzer produces the terms that go into the index** — tokenization + lowercase + stop-word removal + stemming; the same analyzer must run on both documents at index time and queries at search time or results are inconsistent
- **Posting list enables efficient relevance scoring** — stores term frequency, document frequency, and field length; BM25 computes score from posting list data without re-reading documents
- **B-tree cannot support full-text search** — B-trees find exact or range matches on a column; they can't find documents containing a specific word among many other words; inverted index is the required structure
- **Position data in posting lists enables phrase queries** — `match_phrase` requires terms to be adjacent; the inverted index stores term positions within each document to verify adjacency without reading document text

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An inverted index is the data structure that makes full-text search fast. Understanding how it works explains why `match` queries are O(1) lookups rather than O(n) scans.

**Forward index vs inverted index**
- A forward index maps document IDs to their contents — `doc:1 = ["spring", "boot", "java"]` — which means finding all documents containing "boot" requires scanning every document's word list: O(n)
- An inverted index flips this: it maps each unique term to the list of documents containing it — `"boot" -> [doc:1, doc:3, doc:7]` — which means searching for "boot" is a single lookup in the term dictionary: O(1) to find the list, then O(k) to retrieve k matching documents

**How Elasticsearch builds it**
- When a document is indexed, its text fields pass through the analysis pipeline — the analyzer tokenizes the text into terms, applies filters (lowercase, stop-words, stemming), and stores each term with a posting list (the list of document IDs that contain the term)
- `to_tsvector('spring boot framework')` in PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch's analyzer both produce the same conceptual result: a set of normalized tokens with their positions

**Posting lists and relevance scoring**
- The inverted index stores not just which documents contain a term, but how often the term appears in each document and the total frequency across the corpus — which means BM25 relevance scoring can be computed efficiently from the posting list data without re-reading documents
- BM25 (the default scoring algorithm) scores higher for: terms that appear frequently in the document, terms that appear rarely across the corpus (high IDF), shorter documents

**Why full-text search can't use a B-tree**
- A B-tree finds documents where a field equals an exact value or falls in a range — `WHERE title = 'spring boot'` or `WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 100`; it can't find documents where a field contains a word
- The inverted index is the only structure that maps terms to documents efficiently across the full corpus

questions.question: How do you handle Elasticsearch pagination for deep results?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Pagination: Handling Deep Result Sets
questions.direct_answer: Elasticsearch supports three pagination mechanisms. The **from/size** approach is simple but becomes prohibitively expensive beyond 10,000 results because every shard must sort and return from + size results. The **search_after** approach uses a sort value cursor for efficient deep pagination without skipping results. The **scroll API** was designed for bulk data export but is deprecated for user-facing pagination -- search_after is the recommended replacement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand why from/size pagination degrades at depth and can describe the search_after pattern for efficient stateless pagination.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using from/size for unbounded pagination (fetching page 1000 of results), which causes Elasticsearch to retrieve and discard enormous numbers of documents across all shards.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the scatter-gather cost of deep from/size pagination -- each shard returns (from + size) results to the coordinating node, which must sort and discard from of them, so page 1000 of 10 results requires each shard to return 10,010 hits.

sections.title: The Problem: Deep Pagination Performance Collapse
sections.content: A product search API uses Elasticsearch with from/size pagination. Users report that loading page 500 of results is extremely slow -- sometimes timing out. The Elasticsearch cluster CPU spikes on deep page requests, but shallow pages are fast. The system has 3 shards per index.

sections.title: The Broken Approach: from/size at Depth
Root Cause: Scatter-Gather Cost Grows with Page Depth
sections.content: The root cause is that from/size pagination requires all shards to return from + size documents to the coordinating node, which then sorts and discards the first from results. At deep pages, this scatter-gather cost becomes enormous. Elasticsearch enforces a default max_result_window of 10,000 to prevent runaway queries, which is why very deep pagination fails entirely. The problem is architectural: from/size is not designed for deep pagination.

sections.title: The Fix: Cursor-Based Pagination with search_after
Spring Boot Implementation — Cursor Pagination with PIT and search_after
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`from/size` is inefficient at depth** — page 100 requires retrieving 1,000 results per shard and discarding 990; the default 10,000 result window limit is protecting against the cost, not an arbitrary restriction
- **`search_after` for forward-only user pagination** — stateless cursor using last-page sort values; no result window limit; requires a deterministic sort with a unique tiebreaker (`_id` as final sort key)
- **Scroll for bulk data export, not user UI pagination** — maintains a point-in-time snapshot; every open scroll consumes cluster memory; use PIT + `search_after` as the modern replacement
- **PIT + `search_after` is the modern bulk pagination** — `_pit` opens a snapshot; `search_after` pages through it; no per-shard state maintained; cleaner than scroll for ETL pipelines
- **Sort consistency is required for `search_after`** — include a unique field (`_id`) as the final sort key to ensure deterministic ordering; ties in the primary sort key cause missed or duplicated results

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Elasticsearch supports three pagination approaches, and the choice depends on how deep you need to paginate — each has trade-offs that make one clearly better for different use cases.

**from/size — simple but breaks at depth**
- `from: 0, size: 10` returns the first page; `from: 990, size: 10` returns page 100 — but to serve page 100, Elasticsearch must retrieve the top 1,000 results from every shard, merge them, and discard 990 — which means a request for page 1,000 with size 10 moves 10,000 results from each shard, even if there are 20 shards
- The default `index.max_result_window` is 10,000 — requests beyond that fail; this is not a bug, it's protecting against the memory and bandwidth cost of deep pagination

**search_after — cursor-based, forward only**
- `search_after` uses the sort values of the last document in the previous page as a cursor — `"search_after": [1704067200, "doc-id-xyz"]` returns results after that point in the sort order
- This is stateless — no need to track a scroll context; suitable for real-time search results where users page forward; the trade-off is that it's forward-only (no jumping to page 50) and the sort must be deterministic (include a unique tiebreaker like `_id`)

**Scroll API — for bulk export**
- `POST /index/_search?scroll=2m` opens a point-in-time snapshot and returns a `scroll_id`; subsequent requests with that scroll_id return the next batch, always from the same snapshot
- Scroll is designed for bulk data export — exporting all documents, feeding an ETL pipeline — not for user-facing pagination; scroll contexts consume memory on the cluster for the duration of the scroll
- Point-in-time (PIT) with `search_after` is the modern replacement for Scroll: `POST /index/_pit?keep_alive=5m` opens a snapshot; subsequent searches with the PIT ID and `search_after` page through it without maintaining per-shard state

questions.question: What is an Elasticsearch cluster -- nodes, shards, replicas?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Cluster Architecture: Nodes, Shards, and Replicas
questions.direct_answer: An Elasticsearch **cluster is a group of nodes** that collectively store and search data. Data is divided into shards (**primary shards** hold the actual data; **replica shards** are copies for fault tolerance and read throughput). Each shard is a self-contained Lucene index. Nodes take on roles -- master (cluster coordination), data (shard storage), coordinating (query routing) -- and can serve multiple roles in small clusters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain the distribution model and understand the operational implications of shard count, replica count, and node roles.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting too many primary shards at index creation (shards are fixed and cannot be changed without reindexing). Elasticsearch recommends 10-50 GB per shard as a target.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the split-brain problem and how the master election quorum (minimum_master_nodes or cluster.initial_master_nodes in 7.x+) prevents it, and explain the write and read paths across primary and replica shards.

sections.title: Distributed Storage and Search
sections.content: An Elasticsearch cluster provides distributed storage and search by spreading data across nodes as shards. Primary shards accept writes and hold the authoritative copy of data. Replica shards are synchronized copies that serve read requests and provide failover. The cluster's master node maintains the cluster state -- which shards live on which nodes -- and coordinates rebalancing.

sections.title: Cluster Topology and Request Paths
sections.content:
Elasticsearch Cluster (3 nodes, index with 3 primary shards, 1 replica each):

Node 1 (master + data):    [P0] [R1] [R2]
Node 2 (data):             [P1] [R0] [R2]
Node 3 (data):             [P2] [R0] [R1]

P0 = Primary shard 0, R0 = Replica of shard 0
Each shard is a full Lucene index (~10-50 GB target size)

Write path for a document:
1. Client sends to any node (coordinating role)
2. Coordinating node hashes document _id to determine shard: shard = hash(_id) % num_primary_shards
3. Request forwarded to primary shard node
4. Primary writes and replicates to all replica shards
5. ACK returned to client once primary + replicas confirm write

Read path:
1. Coordinating node determines shard using same hash
2. Routes to primary OR any replica (round-robin for load balancing)
3. Returns result to client

sections.title: Master Node
sections.content: The master node manages cluster state: which indices exist, how many shards each has, and which node holds each shard. It coordinates shard allocation and rebalancing when nodes join or leave. In production, designate dedicated master-eligible nodes to prevent master instability under heavy data load. Elasticsearch 7.x introduced cluster.initial_master_nodes to safely bootstrap the cluster and prevent split-brain without requiring a manual quorum setting.

sections.title: Data Nodes
sections.content: Data nodes store shards and execute search and indexing operations. They hold the Lucene indexes on disk. Shard sizing is critical: Elasticsearch recommends 10-50 GB per shard. Under-sharding (too few shards) limits parallelism and makes future scaling difficult. Over-sharding (too many small shards) increases per-query overhead because every shard participates in the scatter-gather even if it holds no matching documents. For a 500 GB index, 10-20 shards is a reasonable starting point.

sections.title: Replica Shards
sections.content: Replica shards are synchronized copies of primary shards. They serve two purposes: fault tolerance (if a data node fails, Elasticsearch promotes a replica to primary) and read throughput (search queries can be served from any replica, distributing load). The number of replicas can be changed at any time without reindexing, unlike primary shard count. For production, set replicas to at least 1. Set replicas to 0 during bulk initial indexing to double write throughput, then restore replicas after.

sections.title: Production Cluster Sizing — Heap, Shard Count, and the 20GB Rule
sections.content:
Designing an Elasticsearch cluster involves a handful of widely-violated rules that show up in every interview about production deployment.

**The 30GB heap ceiling**.
- Elasticsearch should never run with a JVM heap larger than ~30-31GB.
- Above this threshold, the JVM disables compressed object pointers (CompressedOops), causing every object reference to consume 8 bytes instead of 4.
- The doubling of pointer size typically wipes out any benefit from the larger heap and can actually reduce performance.
- If a node needs more than 30GB of memory, the answer is multiple Elasticsearch instances on the same machine (each with its own 30GB heap), not one larger heap.
- The remaining RAM should be left to the OS for filesystem cache, which Lucene relies on heavily for memory-mapped doc values and segments.

**The 50% RAM rule**.
- Heap size should be roughly 50% of physical RAM, capped at 30GB. The other half goes to OS page cache.
- Production clusters that allocate 90% of RAM to heap typically suffer poor query performance because Lucene's memory-mapped files are constantly evicted from cache.
- A node with 64GB RAM should run with a 30GB heap, leaving 34GB for OS cache.

**The 20GB shard size guideline**.
- Each shard should be 10-50GB in size, with 20GB being the sweet spot for most workloads.
- Shards smaller than 1GB waste cluster overhead (each shard maintains its own segments, transaction logs, and metadata); shards larger than 50GB become slow to recover after node failure (the entire shard must be copied to a new node) and take a long time to relocate during rebalancing.
- For an index expected to grow to 1TB, plan for 50 shards of 20GB each.

**The shard count budget**.
- The total shard count per node should be limited to roughly 20 shards per GB of heap.
- A node with 30GB heap can comfortably hold 600 shards before cluster state management overhead becomes a problem.
- Each shard has a fixed cost in heap (segment metadata, query caches, FST term dictionaries) regardless of its size.
- Clusters with thousands of tiny shards (often the result of daily indices that should have been monthly) hit cluster-state-update bottlenecks during master elections and shard movements.

**Replica count for read scaling and durability**.
- The default of 1 replica gives one extra copy for durability and one extra node that can serve reads.
- Increasing to 2 replicas doubles the read throughput for hot indices but triples the storage cost.
- For write-heavy logs, 1 replica is standard; for read-heavy product catalogs, 2-3 replicas can be appropriate.
- Replicas should never exceed `data_node_count - 1` (Elasticsearch will refuse to allocate replicas on the same node as the primary).

**Master node sizing and dedication**.
- In production clusters with more than ~10 data nodes, master responsibilities should be moved to dedicated master nodes.
- Master nodes don't need much CPU or RAM (4-8GB heap is plenty), but they must be reliable: a master that becomes unresponsive due to GC pressure from also serving queries can trigger spurious failover.
- Dedicated masters with only `master: true, data: false` settings provide stability.
- Always use 3 master-eligible nodes (5 for very large clusters) to avoid split-brain via the quorum mechanism (now automatic in 7.x+).

**Coordinating-only nodes for query offloading**.
- For clusters with very high query rates, dedicated coordinating-only nodes (`master: false, data: false, ingest: false`) act as load balancers that aggregate results from data nodes without holding shards themselves.
- This isolates the CPU-intensive aggregation work from data nodes and provides a stable HTTP endpoint for clients (data nodes' addresses change as shards move, but coordinating nodes are stable).

**Hot-warm-cold tiering for time-series data**.
- For logs, metrics, and events, use ILM (Index Lifecycle Management) to automatically migrate older indices to cheaper hardware: hot tier (NVMe SSDs, 1-7 days, ingest + heavy queries), warm tier (SATA SSDs, 7-90 days, occasional queries), cold tier (HDDs or searchable snapshots in S3, 90+ days, rare queries).
- This pattern can reduce storage costs by 80% for a typical observability workload while keeping recent data on fast hardware.
- The `index.routing.allocation.require.data_tier` setting controls which tier each index lives on, and ILM policies move indices automatically based on age.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primary shards = fixed at index creation** — can't be changed after indexing; under-sharding requires re-indexing; target 20-30GB per primary shard as a planning guideline
- **Replica shards serve both HA and read throughput** — replicas run on different nodes; they absorb search queries alongside primaries; adding replicas increases search throughput, not just fault tolerance
- **Set replicas to 0 during bulk indexing** — no replication overhead during heavy writes; restore to 1 after indexing completes; reduces indexing time significantly for large initial loads
- **Fan-out search: every shard runs the query, coordinating node merges** — relevance scoring is per-shard; the coordinating node merges per-shard top-N results into a global top-N; an unbalanced shard with more documents skews the score distribution
- **3 master-eligible nodes prevent split-brain** — quorum requires (N/2 + 1) = 2 of 3 masters; if two nodes can't see the third, one side can still elect a master; never run 2 master-eligible nodes

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An Elasticsearch cluster distributes data across nodes using shards. Every document lives in exactly one primary shard, and sharding is what allows Elasticsearch to scale search horizontally.

**Shards — the unit of distribution**
- An index is divided into N primary shards, each containing a portion of the documents; `number_of_shards: 3` distributes the index across 3 physical Lucene segments across the cluster
- The number of primary shards is fixed at index creation — it cannot be changed after indexing; choose based on expected dataset size, targeting 20-30GB per shard as a practical guideline
- Search queries fan out to all shards in parallel — each shard executes the query locally and returns its top results; the coordinating node merges and ranks the per-shard results into the final response

**Replicas — for HA and read throughput**
- Each primary shard has zero or more replica shards — `number_of_replicas: 1` means every primary has one replica on a different node
- Replica shards also serve search requests — which means adding replicas increases read throughput, not just durability; a cluster with 3 primaries and 1 replica per primary has 6 shards total serving search requests
- Replica count can be changed anytime — set to 0 during bulk indexing for speed (no replication overhead), then restore to 1 after

**Node roles**
- Master-eligible nodes coordinate cluster state changes — shard allocation, index creation, node joins; one is elected as the active master
- Data nodes store shards and execute queries and indexing — the compute-and-storage nodes; scale horizontally as data grows
- Coordinating-only nodes receive client requests, fan them out to data nodes, and merge results — useful to offload merge work from data nodes at high query volume

A minimum production cluster has 3 master-eligible nodes (to form a quorum and prevent split-brain) and separate data nodes scaled to the dataset size.

questions.question: How do you aggregate data in Elasticsearch?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Aggregations: How to Aggregate and Analyze Data
questions.direct_answer: Elasticsearch **aggregations compute analytics** over search results in the same request as the query. There are three types: **bucket aggregations** group documents into buckets (terms, date_histogram, range); **metric aggregations** compute values over a bucket (avg, sum, min, max, cardinality); and pipeline aggregations compute from the output of other aggregations. Aggregations run over the same filtered dataset as the query, enabling faceted analytics.

sections.title: Aggregations as an Analytics Engine
sections.content: Elasticsearch aggregations are a framework for computing grouped analytics over a set of documents -- equivalent to SQL GROUP BY with aggregate functions, but more powerful because they support arbitrary nesting. Aggregations execute in the same request as a search query, letting you retrieve both matching documents and faceted analytics in a single round-trip.

sections.title: Nested Bucket and Metric Aggregations
Building Multi-Level Aggregations for Analytics Dashboards
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`terms` aggregation = GROUP BY for Elasticsearch** — groups by a `keyword` field's distinct values and returns count per value; field must be `keyword` (not `text`) for `terms` to work
- **`date_histogram` for time-series analytics** — groups by calendar interval (day, week, month); the foundation of time-series dashboards; combine with metric sub-aggregations for value-per-period charts
- **Sub-aggregations nest for multi-dimensional analytics** — `date_histogram` > `terms` > `avg` gives average value per category per month in one query; no post-processing needed
- **`cardinality` approximates distinct count with HyperLogLog** — efficient; ~5% error rate; exact distinct count requires fetching all values; use `cardinality` for large-scale "how many unique users" queries
- **Aggregations run in the same request as the query** — filter documents with a `bool.filter` query, aggregate over the filtered set; one round trip returns both search results and analytics

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Elasticsearch aggregations compute analytics over search results in the same request as the query — you get matching documents and computed metrics or buckets in one round trip.

**Bucket aggregations — group documents**
- `terms` aggregation groups documents by a field's distinct values — `agg: { by_status: { terms: { field: "status" } } }` returns counts per status value; similar to SQL's `GROUP BY status`
- `date_histogram` groups documents into time buckets — `{ calendar_interval: "month" }` counts documents per month; the foundation of time-series charts and dashboards
- `range` groups by a numeric range — `{ ranges: [{ to: 100 }, { from: 100, to: 500 }, { from: 500 }] }` distributes documents into price bands

**Metric aggregations — compute values**
- `avg`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `stats` (all five in one) compute aggregates over a numeric field — `{ avg_price: { avg: { field: "price" } } }` gives the mean price across matching documents
- `cardinality` approximates the number of distinct values using HyperLogLog — not exact, but accurate to within ~5% and far more efficient than fetching all values to count unique ones
- `percentiles` computes the p50, p75, p95, p99 of a numeric field — essential for latency analysis

**Sub-aggregations — nest to build complex analytics**
- Aggregations can be nested — `date_histogram` per month containing an `avg` metric gives average price per month; this is how you build multi-dimensional analytics in one query
- Each level of nesting runs within the context of its parent bucket — the `avg_price` within `2024-01` computes the average only for January documents

Aggregations run on data in shards without returning all matched documents — which means computing average order value across 100 million orders is fast; you get one number back, not 100 million documents.

questions.question: How do you keep Elasticsearch in sync with your primary database?
questions.title: Keeping Elasticsearch in Sync with the Primary Database
questions.direct_answer: There are three main approaches to syncing **Elasticsearch** with a primary database: dual-write from the application (simple but risks inconsistency), event-driven sync via a message queue (decoupled and reliable), and Change Data Capture (CDC) using tools like Debezium that read the database's transaction log (most reliable, no application changes required). CDC is the production-recommended approach for large-scale or consistency-critical systems.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the consistency risks of dual-write and can describe more robust sync patterns that handle failures gracefully.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Dual-writing directly from the application without any fallback mechanism, so a failed Elasticsearch write silently leaves the search index stale with no retry or alerting.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how Debezium CDC reads the PostgreSQL WAL (write-ahead log) to capture every committed change and streams it to Kafka, which then drives the Elasticsearch indexer -- ensuring no event is ever lost even if Elasticsearch is temporarily unavailable.

sections.title: The Sync Challenge
sections.content: Elasticsearch is typically used as a secondary read store, with a relational database as the source of truth. This means every change in the primary database must be reflected in Elasticsearch, but the two systems cannot participate in a single ACID transaction. The sync mechanism must handle failures, retries, and ordering to maintain eventual consistency between the stores.

sections.title: Step 1: Dual-Write from the Application (Simple, Fragile)
Step 2: Event-Driven Sync via Kafka (Decoupled, Reliable)
Step 3: Change Data Capture with Debezium (Production-Recommended)
sections.content:
Debezium reads PostgreSQL's write-ahead log (WAL) and publishes every committed INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE as a structured event to Kafka.
- No application code changes are required -- Debezium captures changes at the database level, ensuring nothing is missed even if the application crashes.
- A Kafka Connect sink connector or a custom consumer writes events to Elasticsearch.
- This is the most reliable pattern because the WAL is the definitive record of every committed change, ordered and complete.

sections.title: Step 4: Reconciliation and Recovery
sections.content:
Regardless of the sync approach, implement a periodic reconciliation job that compares a hash or checksum of PostgreSQL records against Elasticsearch documents and re-indexes any discrepancies.
- This catches any events lost due to bugs, configuration changes, or infrastructure failures.
- Run reconciliation daily during low-traffic periods.
- Also implement a full reindex procedure -- using the Elasticsearch Reindex API or a bulk scroll + index job -- that can rebuild the entire search index from the database in case of catastrophic index corruption or mapping changes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Dual-write: simple but has a consistency gap** — application writes to both stores; if the Elasticsearch write fails after a database success, the index is stale with no automatic repair; requires application-level retry and reconciliation
- **CDC with Debezium + Kafka: the production-grade approach** — reads from the database WAL/binlog; Kafka retains events during Elasticsearch downtime; consumer catches up when restored; no data loss window
- **Scheduled ETL: simple but limited freshness** — `WHERE updated_at > watermark` re-indexes changed records; freshness limited by schedule interval; acceptable for reference data, not for frequently-changing records
- **Hard-delete tracking is the ETL gap** — `updated_at` filtering misses deleted rows; soft-delete with `deleted_at` allows ETL to capture deletes; hard-delete requires CDC or application-level tombstone records
- **Periodic full re-index as a safety net** — regardless of sync strategy, schedule a full re-index (weekly or monthly) to correct any accumulated drift; use index aliases to cut over without downtime

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Keeping Elasticsearch in sync with a primary relational database is a distributed systems problem: you have two stores that must stay consistent, and writes happen to one at a time. The three main approaches each have different failure modes.

**Dual-write — application writes to both**
- The application writes to PostgreSQL (or MySQL), then immediately writes to Elasticsearch — which means both stores are updated in the same request
- The failure mode: if the database write succeeds but the Elasticsearch write fails (network error, Elasticsearch node down), the data exists in the database but not in search — and there's no automatic retry; the developer must handle this case explicitly with retries, dead-letter queues, or periodic reconciliation
- Not recommended for high-reliability requirements; acceptable when the search index is "best-effort" and a reindex can repair inconsistency

**CDC with Debezium — event-driven from the database log**
- Debezium captures every row-level change from the database's WAL (PostgreSQL) or binlog (MySQL) and publishes it to Kafka as a change event; a consumer reads from Kafka and applies the change to Elasticsearch
- The advantage: Debezium reads from the database log, which is append-only and reliable — even if the Elasticsearch consumer is down, Kafka retains the events until the consumer is ready; no data is lost during Elasticsearch downtime
- This is the production-grade approach for teams that need reliable sync without dual-write complexity

**Scheduled ETL — simple but delayed**
- A scheduled job queries the database for records changed since the last run and re-indexes them in Elasticsearch — `WHERE updated_at > ?` with a stored watermark
- Simple to implement and reason about; the downside is that freshness is limited by the schedule interval — a 5-minute schedule means search results can be up to 5 minutes stale; not suitable for search on data that changes frequently

Use CDC for reliable production sync; dual-write only for low-stakes applications; scheduled ETL only for reference data that changes infrequently.

questions.question: What are Elasticsearch analyzers and tokenizers?
questions.title: Elasticsearch Analyzers and Tokenizers Explained
questions.direct_answer: An **analyzer** is a pipeline that transforms raw text into indexed terms. It consists of a character filter (pre-processing), a tokenizer (splits text into tokens), and token filters (post-processing: lowercase, stop words, stemming, synonyms). The tokenizer is the core component that determines where term boundaries are. Analyzers are applied both at **index** time (building the inverted index) and query time (parsing the search query), and both must use the same analyzer for consistent matching.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how analyzers affect what gets stored in the inverted index and why the same analyzer must be applied at both index time and query time.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using different analyzers at index time and query time, causing queries to generate terms that do not match the stored indexed terms.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the test endpoint -- POST /_analyze -- for debugging analyzer behavior, and describe use cases for custom analyzers such as autocomplete (edge_ngram tokenizer), case-insensitive exact match (keyword + lowercase filter), and synonym expansion.

sections.title: The Analyzer Pipeline
sections.content: When Elasticsearch indexes a text field, it passes the raw string through an analyzer pipeline that produces a list of terms stored in the inverted index. The same pipeline runs at query time to produce comparable terms from the search query. If index-time and query-time analyzers differ, a query for 'Running' might produce the term 'running', but the indexed term is 'run' (stemmed), causing a miss.

sections.title: Built-in and Custom Analyzer Behavior
Building Custom Analyzers for Real-World Search Requirements
Testing and Debugging Analyzer Behavior
sections.content:
Analyzer misconfiguration is the most common cause of "search returns no results" bugs. Elasticsearch provides the `_analyze` API for testing exactly how text is tokenized — use it before deploying mapping changes.

```bash
# Test how the standard analyzer tokenizes text
POST /my-index/_analyze
{
  "analyzer": "standard",
  "text": "Spring Boot 3.2 micro-service"
}
# Returns tokens: ["spring", "boot", "3.2", "micro", "service"]

# Test with a custom analyzer
POST /my-index/_analyze
{
  "analyzer": "autocomplete_index",
  "text": "spring"
}
# Returns: ["sp", "spr", "spri", "sprin", "spring"]
```

**Debugging zero-result queries.** When a search returns no results unexpectedly, compare the indexed tokens with the query tokens. Use `_analyze` with the index analyzer on the document text, then with the search analyzer on the query string. The query matches when at least one search token exists in the indexed tokens. If they don't overlap, the analyzer configuration has a mismatch — usually a stemmer reducing words differently at index vs search time, or a missing `lowercase` filter on one side.

**Profile API for performance.** Use `"profile": true` in your search request to see exactly which queries and aggregations are expensive. The profile output shows time spent per shard, per query clause, and per collector. This is invaluable for optimizing complex queries where the overall response is slow but the bottleneck is not obvious — often it's a wildcard query or a deeply nested aggregation causing the issue.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Analyzer runs at both index time and query time** — if a different analyzer processes the document and the query, the tokens don't match; always specify the same analyzer on both the field mapping and `match` queries, or rely on Elasticsearch to use the field's configured analyzer automatically
- **`standard` tokenizes and lowercases; `english` also stems** — use `english` for English content where "running", "runs", and "run" should all match the same query
- **Edge n-gram for autocomplete** — generates all prefix tokens of a term at index time; `match` on the n-gram sub-field matches partial input; define a custom analyzer in index settings and apply to a multi-field mapping
- **Character filter strips noise before tokenization** — remove HTML tags with `html_strip`; normalize Unicode characters; runs before the tokenizer so the tokenizer sees clean text
- **`POST /_analyze` tests the token output** — shows the exact tokens that would be indexed for a given text and analyzer; the fastest way to debug unexpected match or no-match results

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An analyzer is the pipeline that converts raw text into the indexed terms stored in the inverted index. The same analyzer runs at index time and query time — if they differ, the indexed tokens don't match the query tokens and searches return no results.

**The three stages of analysis**
- Character filter: pre-processes the raw text before tokenization — strips HTML tags, replaces special characters; optional stage, often omitted
- Tokenizer: splits text into tokens — `standard` tokenizer splits on whitespace and punctuation, lowercases; `edge_ngram` tokenizer generates prefix tokens for autocomplete
- Token filter: transforms the token stream — lowercase filter normalizes case; stop filter removes "the", "a", "is"; stemmer reduces "running" to "run" so all forms match

**Built-in analyzers**
- `standard` is the default — splits on whitespace and punctuation, lowercases; good for general English text; doesn't stem
- `english` adds stemming and stop-word removal on top of standard — "running", "runs", "ran" all match the stemmed token "run"; recommended for English content where morphological matching is needed

**Custom analyzers for autocomplete**
- Edge n-gram tokenizer generates prefix tokens — indexing "spring" produces ["s", "sp", "spr", "spri", "sprin", "spring"]; which means `match: { name.autocomplete: "spri" }` matches "spring" because "spri" is one of its indexed tokens
- Define a custom analyzer in the index settings and apply it to a multi-field mapping: `name.keyword` for exact match, `name.text` for full-text, `name.autocomplete` for prefix search

questions.title: MongoDB Atlas Search vs Elasticsearch
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB Atlas Search is a full-text search engine built directly into MongoDB Atlas, powered by Apache Lucene. **Elasticsearch** is a standalone, distributed search and analytics engine also built on Lucene. Atlas Search eliminates the need to sync data to a separate **cluster**, is simpler operationally, and integrates naturally with MongoDB aggregation pipelines. Elasticsearch offers more advanced search features, richer analytics (Kibana), and is better suited to cross-source or high-scale dedicated search workloads.

interviewer_intent.testing: Assess architectural judgement around search infrastructure, understanding of operational complexity trade-offs, and whether the candidate knows Atlas Search exists as a first-class alternative to running a separate Elasticsearch cluster when the primary store is MongoDB.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Elasticsearch is always required for search because it is the most-known tool. For teams already on MongoDB Atlas with moderate search needs, Atlas Search removes an entire service (no sync pipeline, no separate cluster, no dual-write bugs) while providing 80% of Elasticsearch's features.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the decision framework: Atlas Search wins when search is a secondary feature on MongoDB-resident data; Elasticsearch wins when search is the product, when you need the full Lucene query DSL (span queries, custom scoring scripts, advanced aggregations), or when you're already running ES for logs/observability and can consolidate.

sections.title: Atlas Search vs Elasticsearch Overview
sections.content:
Full-text search is fundamentally different from exact-match database queries.
- Both Atlas Search and Elasticsearch use Apache Lucene under the hood, providing inverted indexes, relevance scoring (BM25), fuzzy matching, faceting, and language-aware text analysis.
- The key difference is operational: Atlas Search runs inside your MongoDB Atlas cluster, shares the same data, and is queried using the familiar $search aggregation stage.
- Elasticsearch is a separate cluster you must provision, and you must keep its data in sync with your primary store — typically via a CDC pipeline or Kafka connector.

MongoDB Atlas Search integrates Apache Lucene directly into the MongoDB query engine, allowing full-text search, faceted search, autocomplete, and fuzzy matching without deploying a separate search cluster. Queries are expressed as aggregation pipeline stages (`$search`, `$searchMeta`), and results can be combined with standard pipeline stages like `$match`, `$group`, and `$lookup` in a single query.

Elasticsearch is a dedicated search engine built on Lucene with deeper capabilities: custom analyzers, complex scoring with function_score, nested/parent-child documents, and a mature ecosystem of tools (Kibana, Beats, Logstash). It requires operating a separate cluster, synchronizing data from MongoDB via change streams or ETL, and managing two schemas.

Choose Atlas Search when your search requirements are moderate (full-text, autocomplete, basic facets) and you want to avoid the operational overhead of a separate search cluster. Data stays in MongoDB, consistency is automatic, and the developer experience is simpler.

Choose Elasticsearch when you need advanced features: complex relevance tuning, custom analyzers for multiple languages, geospatial queries combined with text search, log analytics (ELK stack), or when search query volume is high enough to warrant dedicated infrastructure that scales independently of your primary database.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Atlas Search is Lucene-based, co-located with data** — runs on the same Atlas nodes; no separate cluster to manage; no sync pipeline needed; data is searchable near-immediately after write
- **Elasticsearch provides more control for complex search** — multi-index federation, fine-grained relevance tuning, custom analyzers, and high-volume search throughput at dedicated infrastructure scale
- **Sync to Elasticsearch introduces an eventual consistency window** — dual-write, CDC, or ETL each have failure modes; Atlas Search eliminates this by being in the same system
- **Choose Atlas Search for operational simplicity on Atlas** — if already on Atlas and search requirements are standard (text, fuzzy, autocomplete), Atlas Search avoids an entire separate service
- **PostgreSQL full-text search first for simple cases** — add a dedicated search engine only after validating that the simpler built-in option is insufficient for the actual requirements

sections.title: How to Explain Atlas Search vs Elasticsearch
sections.content:
If you're already on MongoDB Atlas and need full-text search — autocomplete, relevance ranking, faceted navigation — Atlas Search is worth evaluating before adding Elasticsearch as a separate service.

**Atlas Search — built into Atlas, powered by Lucene**
- Atlas Search runs on the same nodes as MongoDB data and uses Apache Lucene under the hood — which means it provides the same text analysis capabilities as Elasticsearch (tokenization, stemming, fuzzy matching, autocomplete) without a separate sync pipeline
- Because it's co-located with the data, there's no eventual consistency lag between writes and search visibility — writes indexed through Atlas Search are typically searchable within a short window, and in some configurations near-immediately

**Elasticsearch — the standalone option**
- Elasticsearch is the industry standard for complex search scenarios: multi-index search, custom relevance tuning, complex aggregation pipelines for analytics, and very high query volumes
- The operational downside: Elasticsearch is a separate cluster to deploy and maintain, and keeping it in sync with the primary database requires a sync strategy — dual writes from the application, CDC via Debezium, or a scheduled ETL job; each has failure modes

**When to choose which**
- Choose Atlas Search when you're already on MongoDB Atlas, the search requirements are straightforward, and you want to avoid a separate sync pipeline; the operational simplicity is the biggest advantage
- Choose Elasticsearch when you have complex relevance requirements, multiple data sources feeding one search index, very high search throughput, or teams with existing Elasticsearch expertise
- Choose neither when PostgreSQL full-text search covers your needs — adding any search service adds operational overhead; validate that simpler tools are insufficient first
